newsitem.title: USA: Dollar/mark ends firmer in U.S. amid EMU doubts.
newsitem.headline: Dollar/mark ends firmer in U.S. amid EMU doubts.

text.p: The dollar closed a volatile week higher against the mark, bolstered by lingering concern about plans for a single European currency, a rebound in prices of Wall Street stocks and comments from a key U.S. financial official, dealers and analysts said.
A proposal by the German government to revalue the Bundesbank's currency and gold reserves sparked a fierce row between government and central bank officials.
The revaluation would free up cash that could be used to slash Germany's budget deficit and help the nation qualify for the proposed single European currency or "Euro".

But Buba has objected saying it infringed on the bank's independence. On Friday, Bundesbank council member Reimut Jochimsen said the government's plans to revalue currency and gold reserves marked a "dramatic conflict" with the central bank that must be played out fully in public.
"The market recognizes that the Bundesbank isn't going to take this gold revaluation plan lightly," said Brian McCarthy, a market analyst at Ruesch International.
"That means we are going to see a barrage of statements from the Bundesbank that will question the viability of the Euro with out the right fiscal underpinnings," McCarthy said.
"So, when ever the value of the euro comes under doubt, of course, they sell marks for dollars and sterling," McCarthy added.

The Dow Jones industrial average had initially tumbled 88 points on Friday after Intel Corp warned it expected revenues in the second quarter to decline five to 10 percent from the previous quarter. Yet the Dow rebounded, which prompted some traders who had previously sold dollars to rush and buy them back, according to traders.
The dollar soared towards 1.71 marks before retreating.
The dollar fetched 1.7050/60 marks at the close, up from 1.7010/15 marks at the open. Against the yen, the dollar edged lower to 116.20/30 from 116.40/45.

Further support for the dollar emerged in comments by William McDonough, president of the New York Federal Reserve Bank. In response to a question at the World Forex Conference in Toronto, McDonough said a strong dollar is in the interest of the United States.
While traders are accustomed to hearing U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin tout the virtues of a strong dollar, McDonough's remarks took some by surprise.

"Generally, you don't hear the Fed people saying that," said Cynthia Cooley, a foreign exchange analyst and trader at United Gulf Bank of Bahrain in Boston. "This is a new person saying it and that kind of made people sort of sit up and pay attention."

The final round of French general elections this Sunday has also garnered much attention in the foreign exchange market. The French Socialists party and its leftist allies scored an impressive showing in the first round of elections on May 25.

The outcome of the runoff vote this weekend will be scrutinized for any potential impact on plans for the proposed single European currency or European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU). The Socialists favor a less stringent interpretation of the standards that have to be met in order to qualify for EMU.

"If the Socialists do get in, that could certainly have implications for French monetary policy, for EMU. It could throw the whole European thing off track presumably," said Frank Pusateri, a vice president of corporate foreign exchange at Mellon Bank in Boston.
Elsewhere, the dollar finished at 1.4140/50 Swiss francs, up from 1.4100/07 francs at the opening.
Sterling rose to $1.6405/15 from $1.6378/88.
The dollar fell to Canadian $1.3770/80 from C$1.3824/29.
The Australian dollar closed at $0.7598/03.
-- Donna Sells 212-859-1668
